analysis.one_liner: Bars the government from leasing federal land for oil and gas when the land has little or no chance of production.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee on the day it was introduced and received no hearing, no vote, and no action before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The government regularly auctions off federal land for oil and gas drilling even when that land has little or no potential to actually produce oil or gas. Companies can pick up these cheap 'speculative' leases just to hold or trade them, tying up land that could be used for grazing, recreation, and wildlife, while taxpayers collect almost nothing. This bill would require the Bureau of Land Management to assess each parcel's real drilling potential first, and to stop offering land designated as low- or no-potential for lease, with narrow exceptions for wells that protect neighboring producing wells.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently fund issuing and managing leases on land that rarely produces; and users of public land — ranchers, hikers, hunters, and wildlife — who lose out when low-value oil leases lock up acreage for other uses.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Bureau of Land Management to complete an assessment of each parcel's oil and gas potential, parcel by parcel, before offering land for lease, and to publish a map of that assessment [S2].

Prohibits offering for lease any federal land designated in the assessment as having low or no potential for oil and gas development, except for narrow drainage-protection cases or a tightly limited variance process capped at one variance per applicant per five years [S3].
Requires public notice, a published request for information, and at least 60 days of public review and comment before the assessments and any variances are finalized [S3].

The bill's findings state that low- and no-potential land is frequently leased at or near the minimum bid and rarely produces, so taxpayers receive minimal revenue, and that such leases limit recreation, grazing, and wildlife uses of the same land [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies, which could no longer acquire cheap leases on land with low or no drilling potential to hold or trade speculatively; the industry also bears the cost of more detailed pre-leasing assessments.

drawbacks.text: The bill would restrict leasing on land the government has judged low-potential, and its exceptions apply only to small parcels near producing wells, so producers argue it forecloses leases that might later prove productive and modestly reduces domestic drilling activity [S3].

The added assessment, mapping, public-comment, and update requirements (updates required at least every 15 years) create new administrative workload for the Bureau of Land Management and could slow lease sales in areas awaiting an assessment [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that federal lease sales contribute revenue and energy supply, and that the bill trades some near-term leasing activity for administrative rigor — which is why the bill includes a variance process for applicants who can document a case that leasing serves the public interest [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core bargain is straightforward: stop spending public money auctioning and managing leases on land that almost never produces, and free that land for other uses. The cost is a slower, more paperwork-heavy leasing process and slightly less acreage available to drillers, largely on parcels with little commercial prospect anyway. The bill keeps exceptions for real drilling cases and leaves all existing environmental review intact. On balance it favors taxpayers and other land users over lease speculators.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never scheduled a hearing or vote, and the bill died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Susie Lee of Nevada introduced the bill on May 16, 2023 [S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Natural Resources, whose approval would be needed before the full House could consider it [S5].
No further action appears in the bill's record: no markup, no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action [S5].
The bill attracted six cosponsors, all Democrats, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the bill still in committee [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies keep their ability to acquire cheap speculative leases on low-potential federal land, and taxpayers continue paying the cost of issuing and managing leases that rarely produce.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the End Speculative Oil and Gas Leasing Act of 2023 in the House.

for.name: Six Democratic cosponsors
for.role: House Democrats who cosponsored the bill
for.what_they_did: Added their names in support; no further action on the bill appears in the record.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; the bill sat there its entire life
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on May 16, 2023 and never scheduled a markup, hearing, or vote; no further action is recorded before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party controlling the House floor calendar and committee agendas in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; with the committee and calendar controlled by the majority, the bill had no path forward.

sides.party_line_note: All seven supporters — the sponsor and six cosponsors — were Democrats; no Republican cosponsor appears in the record, and the Republican-controlled committee took no action on the bill [S4].

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies leasing federal land
industries.note: The bill would end their access to cheap leases on federal land with little or no drilling potential, land they can currently hold or trade speculatively at minimum bid. Those leases occupy land taxpayers could use for grazing, recreation, and wildlife, and rarely generate production or revenue.

industries.industry: Outdoor recreation, ranching, and public land users
industries.note: Land no longer tied up by speculative leases stays available for grazing, recreation, and wildlife habitat, uses the bill's findings say current leases limit. Public participation requirements also give these users a formal voice in leasing assessments.

The bill's findings state that low- and no-potential land is leased at or near minimum bid and rarely produces, so taxpayers get minimal revenue while covering the government's cost of issuing and managing those leases.
